pages.statement: $\classBQP \subseteq \classPP$: [[bounded-error-quantum-polynomial-time|BQP]] is contained in [[probabilistic-polynomial-time|PP]] — [[ADH97 - Quantum Computability|ADH97]]. The containment also follows from $\classBQP \subseteq \mathsf{PostBQP} = \classPP$ — [[Aar05 - Quantum computing, postselection, and probabilistic polynomial-time|Aar05]].
pages.sketch: For a polynomial-time quantum machine with rational amplitudes, the acceptance probability is a sum over pairs of computation paths of products of amplitudes; after clearing a common denominator it is the difference of two $\classsharpP$ functions, and comparing it with $1/2$ is a $\classPP$ predicate. ADH97 extend the argument to algebraic amplitudes.

pages.wrong_reason: As stated (CDH hard ⇒ BDH hard), this is not a known theorem in any model. The known direction is the converse: a CDH solver in the base group breaks BDH — from $g^a, g^b$ compute $g^{ab}$, then $e(g^{ab}, g^c) = e(g,g)^{abc}$ — so BDH hardness implies CDH hardness (BDH ⇒ CDH). The migrated bullet's 'BDH is implied by CDH in the generic group model' misreads the unconditional generic-bilinear-group lower bound for BDH (a hardness proof in an idealized model, quantifying over all generic algorithms) as a reduction from CDH; the suspected-errors entry for bilinear-map-assumptions.md line 35 flags exactly this. Correct edge: bdh-to-cdh.
flags: No inverse page bdh-to-cdh exists in content/Reductions/ — worth creating (folklore, fully-black-box: one pairing evaluation turns a base-group CDH solver into a BDH solver).

The unconditional generic-group hardness of BDH is a different fact (a model-scoped lower bound, not an edge from CDH); if wanted it belongs on the assumption page or as a barrier-style note, not as this reduction.

pages.wrong_reason: Direction inverted. The true implication is DDH ⇒ CDH: a CDH solver computes $g^{ab}$ from $(g, g^a, g^b)$ and compares it with the challenge element, breaking DDH, so DDH hardness implies CDH hardness. The converse is not known and fails in gap groups: in symmetric pairing groups DDH is easy while CDH is conjectured hard (Joux–Nguyen), so no reduction CDH ⇒ DDH can hold for all groups. The migrated sentence contradicts its own following gloss, as the suspected-errors entry for decisional-diffie-hellman.md line 12 records. The correct edge already exists as content/Reductions/ddh-to-cdh.md.
flags: Recommend deleting or redirecting this page: ddh-to-cdh.md already covers the true direction, so repairing in place would create a duplicate.

verifier_changes: wrong_reason: replaced the loose 'none can be group-generic' with the precise gap-group argument (the implication fails in symmetric pairing groups, so no reduction holds for all groups)

pages.class_justification: The reduction is fixed in advance and uses the DLOG solver only as an oracle: on a CDH instance it makes one call, whose input $g^x$ has the same distribution as in the DLOG game, and finishes with one exponentiation. No dependence on the solver's code.
pages.statement: If [[computational-diffie-hellman|CDH]] is hard for a group generator $\GrGen$, then [[discrete-logarithm|DLOG]] is hard for $\GrGen$: a DLOG solver yields a CDH solver with the same advantage, so the DLOG assumption is the weaker of the two — folklore.
pages.sketch: Given a CDH instance $(g, g^x, g^y)$, run the DLOG solver on $(g, g^x)$ to obtain $x$ and output $(g^y)^x$. Since $g^x$ is uniform in both games, one call suffices and the reduction succeeds exactly when the solver does.

sources.ref_file_title: GSW13 - Homomorphic Encryption from Learning with Errors Conceptually-Simpler, Asymptotically-Faster, Attribute-Based
sources.authors: Craig Gentry, Amit Sahai, Brent Waters
sources.note: Approximate-eigenvector FHE from LWE; no evaluation key. Springer DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-40041-4_5. Verifier: title, authors, venue and DOI re-confirmed via web search.

pages.class_justification: The hypotheses are assumptions (LWE, and circular security of the constructed scheme itself), not primitives used as oracles; the unbounded variant bootstraps by evaluating the scheme's own decryption circuit. No source assigns an RTV class.
pages.statement: Assuming [[learning-with-errors|LWE]] is hard, there is a bootstrappable homomorphic encryption scheme, hence [[homomorphic-encryption#leveled-fully-homomorphic-encryption|leveled FHE]]; if the scheme is additionally [[circular-security|circular secure]] (secure given encryptions of its own secret key), bootstrapping yields [[homomorphic-encryption|FHE]] for circuits of arbitrary depth — [[BV11 - Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption from (Standard) LWE|BV11]].
pages.sketch: BV11 build an LWE-based scheme whose homomorphic multiplication uses relinearization (key switching) to keep ciphertexts linear in the secret key, and apply dimension-modulus reduction to shrink ciphertexts and the decryption circuit until the scheme can evaluate its own decryption (replacing Gentry's squashing). Publishing encryptions of the secret key (circular security) then enables Gentry-style bootstrapping, which refreshes ciphertext noise by homomorphically evaluating the decryption circuit.
pages.improvements_text:
- Leveled FHE for any a-priori polynomial depth from LWE alone, without bootstrapping, via modulus switching — [[BGV12 - Leveled fully homomorphic encryption without bootstrapping|BGV12]]
- Approximate-eigenvector FHE from LWE: homomorphic operations are matrix operations and no evaluation key is needed — [[GSW13 - Homomorphic Encryption from Learning with Errors Conceptually-Simpler, Asymptotically-Faster, Attribute-Based|GSW13]]

pages.class_justification: The transformation feeds the scheme's own decryption circuit to $\Eval$, so the construction uses the hypothesis scheme's code rather than oracle access to it; neither Gen09 nor follow-up work places it in an RTV class.
pages.statement: Any bootstrappable [[homomorphic-encryption#somewhat-homomorphic-encryption-she|somewhat homomorphic encryption]] scheme — one able to homomorphically evaluate its own augmented decryption circuit — that is [[circular-security|circular secure]] yields [[homomorphic-encryption|FHE]] for circuits of arbitrary depth (Gentry's bootstrapping theorem) — [[Gen09 - Fully homomorphic encryption using ideal lattices|Gen09]]. pages.sketch: The public key includes encryptions of the secret key. To refresh a noisy ciphertext $c$, homomorphically evaluate $\Dec(\cdot, c)$ on the encrypted secret key, producing a fresh encryption of the same plaintext with bounded noise; refreshing after each gate evaluates circuits of any depth.

sources.ref_file_title: BLS04 - Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing (Journal of Cryptology)
sources.authors: Dan Boneh, Ben Lynn, Hovav Shacham
sources.note: Journal version: general co-GDH group pairs $(\GG_1, \GG_2)$ with isomorphism $\psi$, the co-CDH formulation, and the bound $\varepsilon \ge e(q_S+1)\varepsilon'$. Same title as BLS01; filename disambiguated with a venue suffix. Verifier: journal, volume, issue, pages re-confirmed via web search.

pages.class_justification: Fixed construction using only group, hash, and pairing operations; the security reduction runs the forger once as an oracle, programming its random oracle, and extracts a co-CDH solution from the forgery. Fully-black-box shape, in the ROM.
pages.model_justification: The proof models $H$ as a programmable random oracle (BLS01, BLS04); no standard-model proof of BLS is known.
pages.statement: [[digital-signature#bls-signatures|BLS signatures]]: in a bilinear group pair $(\GG_1, \GG_2)$ of prime order $p$ with pairing $e : \GG_1 \times \GG_2 \to \GG_T$ and hash $H : \bits^* \to \GG_1$, $\sk = x \getsr \ZZ_p$, $\pk = g_2^x$, $\Sign(\sk, m) = H(m)^x$, and $\Vrfy$ accepts $(m, \sigma)$ iff $e(\sigma, g_2) = e(H(m), \pk)$. With $H$ a random oracle, the scheme is EUF-CMA secure if [[co-computational-diffie-hellman|co-CDH]] is hard in $(\GG_1, \GG_2)$ — [[BLS01 - Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing|BLS01]], [[BLS04 - Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing (Journal of Cryptology)|BLS04]].
pages.sketch: The reduction receives a co-CDH challenge $(g_2^a, h)$, sets $\pk = g_2^a$, and programs $H$: each new query is answered by $\psi(g_2)^{r}$ with known $r$, except with probability $1/(q_S+1)$ by $h \cdot \psi(g_2)^{r}$, where $\psi : \GG_2 \to \GG_1$ is the efficiently computable isomorphism of the co-GDH definition. Signing queries on points of the first kind are answered by $\psi(g_2^a)^{r}$; a forgery $\sigma$ on a point of the second kind yields $h^a = \sigma / \psi(g_2^a)^{r}$.
pages.security_loss: factor $e(q_S+1)$ over the co-CDH advantage: a forger with advantage $\varepsilon$ making $q_S$ signing queries yields a co-CDH solver with advantage $\varepsilon/(e(q_S+1))$ and $O(q_H + q_S)$ extra group operations
pages.improvements_text: - Journal version with the general co-GDH framework, the asymmetric-pairing co-CDH formulation, and the explicit $e(q_S+1)$ loss — [[BLS04 - Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing (Journal of Cryptology)|BLS04]]

pages.wrong_reason: GMW87's semi-honest protocol is built from oblivious transfer, not from commitments; commitments (via zero-knowledge proofs for NP) enter only in the GMW compiler lifting semi-honest security to malicious security. As stated, 'COM is complete for MPC in the semi-honest model' is not a known theorem: commitments follow from OWFs (Naor from PRG, HILL), semi-honest 2PC for all functionalities implies semi-honest OT, and OT is black-box separated from OWFs (Impagliazzo–Rudich), so the claim would place OT in Minicrypt. The suspected-errors entries for commitment-scheme.md line 64 and secure-multi-party-computation.md line 64 record the same error. Correct GMW87-adjacent edges: OT ⇒ semi-honest MPC (GMW87), and {ZK-from-COM, semi-honest MPC} ⇒ malicious MPC (the GMW compiler) — neither is what this page states.

The suspected-errors entry for commitment-scheme.md line 65 records this. Correct edges already exist: content/Reductions/ot-to-com.md and content/Reductions/ot-to-mpc-kil88.md.
